summary.text:
The LOBO detail is the reason to read this. Oldham publishes what it was actually offered: £5m from FMS Wertmanagement called at a proposed 7.67% and repaid within a week, and a Dexia loan called at 6.70% and repaid in December. Almost nobody publishes the offered rate — Wolverhampton is the only other council we hold that does — and between them they put hard numbers on what lenders are asking across the sector and borrowers are refusing.

It is not over. £39.000m of the remaining £76.000m carries call dates inside twelve months, £9.000m with Dexia across two loans and £20m across Danske Bank, Just Retirement and KBC. Dexia now appears in our library at Kent, Tameside, Newcastle and Oldham.

The balance sheet closes exactly on two paths: CFR £581.037m less £211.360m of PFI is the £369.677m borrowing CFR, and less £259.959m of borrowing is the £109.718m of internal borrowing they state. The liability benchmark puts existing borrowing above the benchmark today — £259.996m against £200.325m — and forecasts it below by 2027.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Audit Committee on 22 July, ahead of Cabinet on 7 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. Your Table 1 closes exactly: CFR of £581.037m less £211.360m of PFI and other debt liabilities gives the £369.677m borrowing CFR, and less external borrowing of £259.959m gives the £109.718m of internal borrowing you state. The liability benchmark rebuilds the same way — £347.724m of loans CFR less £167.399m of balance sheet resources is £180.325m, plus the £20.000m liquidity allowance gives £200.325m.

We wrote because of paragraph 2.4.10, and specifically because you published the numbers. £5m from FMS Wertmanagement called on 31 March 2025 at a proposed 7.67% and repaid within a week; a Dexia loan called at a proposed 6.70% and repaid on 23 December. Almost no council publishes the rate it was offered. We have read a lot of LOBO reporting this summer and exactly one other authority does it — Wolverhampton, which was offered 6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26% on three loans and rejected all three, describing the rates as "deliberately set unattractively high so it would not be accepted".

Put your two next to their three and you have the only hard evidence in the sector of what LOBO lenders are actually asking. 6.19% to 7.67%, and every one refused. That is a picture no individual council can see from its own papers, and it is the sort of thing we exist to assemble and publish. We would be glad to send you the cross-council view when we write it up.

It also matters directly to you, because £39.000m of your remaining £76.000m carries call dates inside the next twelve months — £9.000m with Dexia across two loans and £20m spread across Danske Bank, Just Retirement and KBC. Dexia now appears in our library at Kent, Tameside, Newcastle and Oldham, which suggests one lender working systematically through its book rather than four unrelated decisions. Your stated policy at 2.4.11 is to repay at no additional cost if called, funded from cash, alternative sources or the PWLB "always providing that overall savings can be demonstrated" — so the replacement price is the whole question. This afternoon on notice 314/26, PWLB certainty closed at 4.95% for one year, 5.34% at five, 5.83% at ten and 6.38% at twenty. July's sector lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is thin. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Two smaller things. On the DMO's premature repayment curve today your PWLB book prices at about £9.4m of net discount on a £111.8m balance — five loans below par against twelve above, so unusually balanced. Standard caveats: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, only the DMO can quote, and ours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

And your reported 10-year certainty range for the year — 5.38% at the start, 5.72% at the end, 5.13% low, 5.88% high — matches our own series exactly and is identical to four other Arlingclose clients we have read this summer.

On training, four fit Oldham. LOBO loans (legacy) is written for precisely your position, and Debt restructuring sits with it. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, given yours has existing borrowing above the benchmark today and below it by 2027 — that crossing is the useful thing to show members. And Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset) for the £13.610m and the £2m override provision you have decided to keep. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
